1	<!-- Probe Y of the plan review of 2026-11-10 (its section 7.4), run 2026-11-13 by a Fable worker: whether one build of the tree can compile and run a program against the compiler's prelude and against the interpreter's library, with the prelude's run-time value classes kept and a second, re-parented set beside them; done in a scratch worktree, `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) with the rehearsal's patch applied; it works, and this note gives what ran, how the library is selected, every hack, the walls, the cost of the second set and an estimate in rungs; nothing here lands, and the scratch tree's whole diff is `probe-y.patch` beside this report. -->
2	
3	# Probe Y: one build, two libraries
4	
5	**The answer: yes.** One `ant compileAll` of the scratch tree gives a build that compiles and runs the one-line program against the compiler's prelude, as today, and against the interpreter's library, chosen by one environment variable at the compile and at the run. The rehearsal's `Array1` program and its dot loop also run against the interpreter's library in that build, by hand and through the test harness. A sample of the compiled tests passes against the prelude in the same build. No wall stopped the probe.
6	
7	The base is `832f7d0d91`, the rehearsal's. "The rehearsal" is `switch-rehearsal.md`, beside this note; its walls are W1 to W16 and its hacks 1 to 12. "The review" is `explorations/reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`. "The one library" is the interpreter's library.
8	
9	Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.10GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` for the runs by hand and 4 in the harness. Another workflow ran beside the probe; the load was 0.2 at the first build and up to 9.8 later. No timing here is a pair.
10	
11	## 1. What ran
12	
13	All in `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, after one `ant compileAll` (43 s, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`) and the two library orders (section 5).
14	
15	The three programs are the rehearsal's by its description (its section 4); its files were not kept, so they were written again. `Hello` is `run(): () = println("Hello, one library")`.
16	
17	**The prelude** (no variable set, the tree's own `default_repository/caches`):
18	
19	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
20	    Hello, one library                         (both exit 0)
21	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss
22	    Arr.fss:5:6-10: Array1 is undefined.       (exit 255; Dot.fss alike, 2 errors)
23	
24	`Arr` and `Dot` cannot compile against the prelude in any build: it has no array type (row 305).
25	
26	**The one library** (`FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/default_repository/caches-one`, and for each run the rehearsal's flags that switch the verifier off, its W7):
27	
28	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
29	    Hello, one library
30	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Arr
31	    a[5] = 25
32	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Dot.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Dot
33	    dot = 499500.0                             (every command exit 0)
34	
35	With `-verbose:class`, the prelude's run of `Hello` loads no class whose name holds `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` or `FlatStringC`, and the one library's run loads none whose name holds `CompilerBuiltin` or `CompilerLibrary` (each count 0).
36	
37	**Through the harness, against the one library.** Three `.test` files (`link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=` the line above) for the three programs, in one `fortress junit` run with the same three settings:
38	
39	    . run .../ArrOne (1375ms) a[5] = 25
40	    . run .../DotOne (1826ms) dot = 499500.0
41	    OK (6 tests)                               (16 s)
42	
43	**Through the harness, against the prelude, in the same build** (`ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`, on `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests`):
44	
45	- Twelve files chosen for what the second set touches (helpers that raise, the `NN32`, integer, `Char` and `asFloat` helper families, a caught `FileNotFoundException`, two `atomic` tests, one refusal of the code generator): `OK (22 tests)`.
46	- Every seventh file of the folder's sorted list, 125 files: `Tests run: 205, Failures: 4`. The four are `XXXFortToStringRungS`, `XXXGenericFunctionalMethodSelfSecond`, `XXXGenericTraitGenericFunctionalMethod` and `XXXPowNN64CompiledRungE`, each 'Could not load …: Resource not found'. The same four files run alone on the base build's code (`old-fortress.sh … junit`) fail in the same way, `Tests run: 4, Failures: 4`: a file with only a `run` step needs its sibling's jar, which a sample leaves out. So the sample shows no test that the second set disturbed.
47	
48	**What did not run, and what was not tried.** The whole compiled tracks (1,907 tests) were not run against the prelude; the sample is 137 files of 876 in one folder. Walk was not run: the rehearsal's library text breaks it in a scratch tree (its hack 4), and this probe kept that text. A matrix, the library's `DOT` and microGPT stop where the rehearsal stopped (its W15, W16 and section 4); nothing here changes that. The cheaper form that the carriers' review proposes (section 7) was not tried.
49	
50	## 2. How the library is selected
51	
52	One variable, `FORTRESS_LIBRARY`. Unset, everything is as today. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`:
53	
54	- **At the compile.** `WellKnownNames.compiledPathUsesOneLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java`) reads the variable once for the JVM (or `-Dfortress.library=one`). `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java`), which every compiled-path command calls, points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at the one library's names where it is set, and at the prelude's where not.
55	- **At the run.** `bin/fortress_classpath` puts `ProjectFortress/build-one`, the second set's classes, before `ProjectFortress/build`. `bin/run_classpath` builds on that script, so the run's JVM finds the second set's `FZZ32` first. The compile's JVM gets the same class path.
56	- **The caches.** A caches folder holds one library's jars and the programs compiled against it, so the one library has its own: `default_repository/caches-one`, named by hand in `FORTRESS_CACHES`.
57	
58	One JVM serves one library: `NamingCzar`'s tables are filled once, when the class loads, as on the base (`NamingCzar.fortLib`). The harness fits this: its `run` step is a process of its own that inherits the environment, so a test track against the one library is the same harness started with the three settings.
59	
60	### What had to follow the selection
61	
62	| what | file | how it follows |
63	|---|---|---|
64	| the names of the default library | `Shell.java`, `WellKnownNames.java` | by the variable |
65	| the thirteen value classes, with `FValue`, `MutableFValue`, `Utility` and `FException` | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/`; second set in `ProjectFortress/build-one` | two sets of classes under the same names, the class path chooses |
66	| the stores' carriers `FJavaArrayStore`, `FJavaRR64ArrayStore`; the stubs `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, `FortressBuiltin.java`, `FlatStringC.java` | `ProjectFortress/src-one/` | in the second set only |
67	| the helpers' 99 raise strings, and the six of `FortressBufferedReader` and `FortressBufferedWriter` | `runtimeValues/LibraryNames.java`, one copy in each set; `Utility.java` calls it | the strings stay the prelude's; the second set's copy maps them |
68	| the compile's table of carried types (the rehearsal's 15 rows) | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | entered only where the one library is selected, since each row also enters the type's bare name (`NamingCzar.b`), and a test's own `Float` or `Char` would be taken for a carried type |
69	| a carried parent named by its interface (W14); `FlatString`'s class named `fortress/FlatStringC` | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | by the variable |
70	| a carried type's `RTTIc` holds its carrier (W12) | `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` | by the variable |
71	| the tolerant code generator (hack 7): refused declarations left out, a method written twice, a class written twice | `CodeGen.java` (four `catch` blocks), `CodeGenClassWriter.java`, `runtimeSystem/ByteCodeWriter.java` | by the variable: the prelude keeps its refusals |
72	| the search of the trait table (W3) | `scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala` | does not follow: it searches four prelude apis, then the one library's two, and finds only those that the compile loaded |
73	| the run's copy of the table; the wrapper generator's converters | `runtimeSystem/Naming.java`, `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java` | do not follow: each is keyed by a name that holds its library, so both libraries' rows stand together |
74	| the dispatch method's package (W11) | `compiler/OverloadSet.java` | does not follow: the rehearsal's repair, the same for both |
75	
76	The classes of the build that link against a prelude class by name, found by reading the constant pools of `ProjectFortress/build`: the thirteen, `FValue` and `MutableFValue` (their `asString()` returns `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.String`), `Utility` (the constructor it looks up takes that type), `FException` (it calls `FValue.asString()`), and the prelude's own `FZZ32Vector` and `FStringVector`. Every other mention of the prelude in the run time and the helpers is a string.
77	
78	**The second set is the first set under a map of names.** The rehearsal's re-parented classes differ from the base's only in the names of the generated classes that they extend, so the scratch build makes the second set's sources from the first's: `build.xml` copies seventeen files through eight replacements (`CompilerBuiltin.RR64` to `FortressBuiltin.Float`, `CompilerBuiltin.JavaString` to `FlatStringC.FlatString`, and so on, with `CompilerBuiltin.` to `FortressLibrary.` last) and compiles them with `src-one` into `build-one`. One of the eight is a whole clause: the prelude's `FRR32` implements `RR32` and `RR64`, the rehearsal's only `RR32`.
79	
80	## 3. The hacks
81	
82	Each is marked `PROBE Y` in the patch. The rehearsal's twelve are all still in the tree and are not repeated here; nine of them are now behind the variable.
83	
84	1. **The selector is an environment variable read in two places** (`WellKnownNames`, `bin/fortress_classpath`). Proper form: one selector, say an option of the commands that the scripts pass on, or a mark in the program's jar that the run reads, so that a program compiled against one library cannot be run on the other's classes. Today a wrong pairing fails at load with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
85	2. **The one library's caches folder is named by hand.** Proper form: `ProjectProperties.CACHES` and the two scripts take the folder from the selection; `ant cleanCache` and the build's stamp know both folders. Today the build stamps and empties only `default_repository/caches`, so the one library's jars go stale without notice after an edit of the code generator.
86	3. **The second set's sources are made by string replacement in `build.xml`,** one rule a whole clause of one file. Proper form: it depends on the carriers' decision. If the two sets stay equal up to names, the map can stand as a small table; if the one library's carriers get content of their own, they are hand-written files in `src-one`.
87	4. **The raise strings are mapped by prefix** (`LibraryNames.exceptionClass`): `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$X` and `fortress.CompilerLibrary$X` to `fortress.FortressLibrary$X`. Proper form: a helper names an exception by its simple name, and each set's `LibraryNames` gives the component. That edits the 105 strings once, with no change of behaviour for the prelude.
88	5. **The guards around the rehearsal's hacks** (`if (!compiledPathUsesOneLibrary) throw __t`, and the like). They go when the hacks they guard are repaired.
89	6. **`Naming.java`'s table and the converters hold both libraries' rows.** Harmless by their keys. Proper form: they follow the selection as `NamingCzar`'s does, from one table.
90	7. **The build's stamp does not cover `build-one`** (`build.xml`, `implementationFingerprint`). Proper form: it does.
91	8. **The verifier is off for every run against the one library,** as in the rehearsal (W7). With it on, `Hello` dies as there: 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack … FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods'.
92	
93	## 4. The walls, in the order met
94	
95	None stopped the probe. What was met:
96	
97	1. **Each row of the compile's table also enters the type's bare name.** By reading `NamingCzar.b`, before any run; passed by entering the one library's rows only where it is selected. No row; it is a property of row 874's table.
98	2. **`Array1 is undefined` against the prelude** for `Arr` and `Dot`. Row 305.
99	3. **`b[i] := 1.0 i`, with `i` a `ZZ32`, is refused against the one library:** 'Ambiguous coercion in call to operator juxtaposition: of the declarations applicable to an argument of type (RadixPointNumeral[\2,1,10,10\], ZZ32) only by coercion, none is more specific than every other: ((RR64 & {Float}), RR64)->RR64; (QQ, QQ)->QQ.' The rehearsal met it on a model line (its "For the ledger", row 533's kind). Here it is a four-line program. It is on the scratch library, whose `Float` is a trait; `Dot` uses `asFloat(i)` instead.
100	4. **The prelude's bytecode is not the base's, byte for byte** (section 6). No row; row 430 holds the like for walk's messages.
101	5. **Four `XXX` tests with only a `run` step fail in a sample** on both trees (section 1). Not a defect.
102	6. **The verifier** (W7; rows 307 and 695's kind), unchanged.
103	
104	## 5. What the second set costs
105	
106	**Source.** Against `832f7d0d91` the patch touches 28 files (the rehearsal's touched 47): the 105 raise strings and the thirteen classes are back to the base's text.
107	
108	- Hand-written and new for the second set: six files, 221 lines, in `ProjectFortress/src-one/`: the three stubs (174 lines), the two stores' carriers (32) and `LibraryNames` (15). The stubs and the stores' carriers are the rehearsal's; the switch-over needs them on either road.
109	- New for the selection: `LibraryNames` in the first set (9 lines), 2 lines in `Utility.java`, 43 lines of `build.xml`, 9 of `bin/fortress_classpath`, 8 of `WellKnownNames.java`, 7 more in `Shell.java`, and about a dozen guards.
110	- Generated, not kept in git: seventeen files, 638 lines. Kept by hand instead, the second set would be those 638 lines in git, to be edited beside the first set's on every change.
111	
112	**The build.** `ant compileAll` after the edits, with scalac: 43 s; the skill's figure for a build after an edit is 25 to 60 s. With nothing changed: 7.7 s at a load of 9.8, against the skill's "about 4 s"; the second `javac` compiled nothing. `build-one` holds 101 class files, 432 KB.
113	
114	**The library orders**, one after the other in this build:
115	
116	    prelude, five compiles          25 s    (AnyType 4, CompilerBuiltin 12, CompilerLibrary 6, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 1)
117	    one library, fourteen compiles  204 s   (AnyType 18, FortressBuiltin 12, FortressLibrary 84, RangeInternals 41, the other ten 49)
118	
119	The rehearsal gives "about 200 s" for the fourteen, and the skill "100 to 110 s" for the five; the five took 25 s here, on an idle machine. The one library's caches are 70 MB against the prelude's 16 MB.
120	
121	**A gate.** By the figures on file and these: a second library order adds about 200 s to each gate (the review's section 7.2 says the same), once, since the tracks' JVMs fill private caches from it or beside it; how the ant tracks would share it was not built. A test track against the one library costs what its tests cost: three tests took 16 s in one JVM here, most of it the compiles. So the standing cost is of the order of four minutes a gate while the track is small, and grows with the tests moved.
122	
123	**To keep.** While both libraries live: every edit of a first-set file reaches the second through the map without work, if the two stay equal up to names; an edit that should differ between them needs the file moved to `src-one`. Every hack of section 3 that becomes a mechanism (selector, caches, stamp, names table) is code that the prelude's deletion removes again.
124	
125	## 6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler
126	
127	To see whether the second set disturbed the first, the five prelude jars of this tree were compared with the base build's, class by class, after the tree's path was rewritten in each class's constants.
128	
129	    base build's jars against the base build's code, compiled again cold:        590 classes, 590 equal
130	    base build's jars against the base build's code over this tree's sources:    590 equal
131	    base build's jars against this tree's jars:                                  558 equal, 32 differ
132	    this tree's CompilerBuiltin, compiled twice:                                 312 classes, 16 differ
133	    the base build's code with -XX:hashCode=0, and with =1:                      312 classes, 18 differ each
134	
135	The classes that differ hold the same methods in another order, and their dispatch methods test the same types in another order (`javap` of `CompilerBuiltin$EqualTo` and `CompilerBuiltin`). So the order in which the code generator writes methods and dispatch tests follows the JVM's identity hashes. The base's code gives the same bytes on each compile only because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run; a changed hash mode moves the order, and this tree's code gives a different order on each compile. Which of the tree's edits unsettles it was not traced. The rehearsal saw the same for the one library ("Which copy comes first is not stable from one compile to the next", its W6).
136	
137	For probe Y it means that a comparison of bytes cannot show that the prelude is undisturbed; the tests have to. For the work it means that a compiled test can pass or fail with the order (the rehearsal's W6 was such a case), and that no two builds of different code give comparable jars.
138	
139	## 7. Doing it properly, in rungs
140	
141	Given the carriers' decision, which stands first on either road:
142	
143	1. **The selection as a mechanism**: one selector, the caches folder and the stamp that follow it, a mark that stops a wrong pairing, the second library order and a first test track against the one library in the gate, with `Hello` as its first test. One rung. It edits `Shell.java`, `ProjectProperties.java`, the scripts, `build.xml` and the gate's script, and no file of the code generator.
144	2. **The second set**: the stubs, the stores' carriers, the names table for the raise strings, and the set itself, by the map or by hand as the decision says; `NamingCzar`'s, `Naming`'s and the converters' tables from one table that follows the selection. One rung, or two if the carriers are written by hand with content of their own. This is the rehearsal's W2 work done beside the prelude's classes and not in their place; it is not work added to W2.
145	
146	So two rungs, perhaps three, and the review's "2 or 3 more for the second set" (its section 7.2) holds or is slightly high: most of what the second set needs, the switch-over needs anyway. After these two, each of the rehearsal's other walls that only the switch shows (W3, W4, W11, W12 to W14) is one rung with a test on the one library, on `main`, under the gate.
147	
148	**Against the carriers' review** (`explorations/reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, way C and its point on the review's 7.1). That review says, by reading, that "one build serves one library" holds only for hand-written carriers that extend generated classes, and that under its way C in form 2 (the code generator writes the carrier over a hand-written payload class that names no library) no second set is needed. This tree's evidence agrees in part and cannot tell the rest:
149	
150	- It agrees on where the tie is. The two sets differ in nothing but the names of the generated classes that the thirteen extend, and the `String` in `FValue.asString()`. A payload class that extends nothing generated has no such name.
151	- It adds one thing that way C's form 2 must also free: `FValue` and `MutableFValue` themselves name the prelude's `String` in `asString()`'s result, and `Utility` and `FException` link against it. A payload class that extends `FValue` inherits that name. So "names no library" needs `asString()` taken out of `FValue` or typed at `Any`; by reading, not tried.
152	- It cannot tell whether the code generator can write a native object over a payload class; that is way C's own three rungs and was not tried here. The session's room went to the main result, the tests and section 6.
153	- If way C in form 2 is taken, rung 2 above shrinks to the names table and the tables' following, and rung 1 stays as it is: the selection, the caches and the gate's second order are needed in any form.
154	
155	**What I could not learn.**
156	
157	- Whether all 1,907 compiled tests pass against the prelude in this build. The sample found nothing; section 6 says why bytes cannot stand in for the tests.
158	- Which edit makes this tree's order of methods vary from compile to compile, and whether the variation ever changes a result under the prelude.
159	- How the ant tracks, with their private caches, would take a second library order.
160	- Whether walk, the count stage and the distance stage are untouched: they run the same build, and none was run. By reading, the guards leave them as they were, since they do not set the variable; the rehearsal's library text is what breaks walk here.
161	- Anything about a JVM that serves both libraries at once. This design does not try it.
162	
163	## Decisions
164	
165	- **Two sets under the same class names, chosen by the class path,** not a second set under new names chosen inside the JVM. The alternatives: new names (a second package), which every place that names a carrier would have to follow: the code generator's literals, `equalityRule`'s `instanceof`, the converters, the loader's tables; or one class that implements both libraries' interfaces, which Java's single superclass forbids for the springboard. Evidence: the run's class path is already assembled by a script with the caches first (`bin/run_classpath`), and the run is a JVM of its own. No decision of the curator covers it; the review's 7.2 says only "a second set … chosen by the world that the compile command and the run select".
166	- **The second set made by a map of names in the build,** not kept by hand. Evidence: the rehearsal's seventeen files equal the base's under eight replacements (checked with `diff`, one file needing the clause). It makes the cost visible; section 3 marks it as a hack.
167	- **Every hack of the rehearsal's put behind the selector,** also where it looked harmless, so that the prelude's compile runs the base's code paths. `OverloadSet`'s four names (W11) were left for both: the rehearsal calls them the repair.
168	- **A wider sample of tests in place of the byte comparison,** once section 6 showed that bytes vary on their own.
169	
170	## Defects, drafted for the ledger
171	
172	- **The order in which the code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests follows the JVM's identity hashes, so the compiled prelude differs from compile to compile once anything moves the hash sequence.** Status NEGATIVE-VERIFIED; class implementation gap (code generator). Reproducer: compile `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` cold on `832f7d0d91` twice, the second time with `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:hashCode=0`: 18 of 312 classes differ, among them `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$EqualTo` (its `CMP` dispatch tests `Unordered` before `TotalComparison` in one and after in the other) and `fortress/CompilerBuiltin` itself. Without the flag, two compiles are equal. Seen on the compiled path only; row 430 is walk's sibling, F-232 the tree's hashes. Notes: the rehearsal's W6 ("which copy comes first is not stable") is the same cause; no site was traced.
173	- **A numeral with a radix point times a `ZZ32` value is tied between `RR64` and `QQ` against the one library** (row 533's kind): `a: Array1[\RR64,0,8\] = array1[\RR64,8\]()` then `a[i] := 1.0 i` in a `seq` loop. Seen under the compile command with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` on the scratch library, where `Float` is a trait; the rehearsal's entry says the same of a model line and asks for a check on an unhacked library. This probe adds the small program, not that check.
174	- **`fortress compile` of a component whose jar is missing and whose analysis is cached writes no jar and exits 0.** Met with `old-fortress.sh`: the private caches were the base's copy, the five prelude jars were deleted, the five compiles exited 0, and `bytecode_cache/` stayed empty. From an empty caches folder the same five compiles write the five jars. The skill's `build-and-caches.md` describes "all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known"; this may be that cause. Not traced further.
175	
176	## Sentences of the specification made false
177	
178	None: nothing lands.
179	
180	## For FACTS
181	
182	- **One build can serve the compiled path with either library: the prelude's thirteen value classes as they are, and a second set of the same names in a second class folder that the run's class path puts first; shown in a scratch tree on `832f7d0d91` with the rehearsal's hacks, where `Hello` runs on both, and an `Array1` program and a dot loop on the one library, by hand and through `fortress junit`.** It means the review's option A2 exists. No test holds it, since nothing landed; the commands and output are in section 1. The second set's classes equal the first's under a map of eight names (section 2).
183	- **The classes of the build that link against a prelude class by name are the thirteen value classes, `FValue`, `MutableFValue`, `Utility`, `FException`, `FZZ32Vector` and `FStringVector`; every other mention of the prelude in the run time and the helpers is a string (105 raise strings).** Shown by the constant pools of `ProjectFortress/build` on `832f7d0d91` (section 2).
184	- **The bytes of the compiled prelude depend on the JVM's identity hashes** (section 6): 590 of 590 classes equal between two compiles of the base's code, 18 of 312 different under another hash mode.
185	- **The one library's order of fourteen compiles took 204 s and the prelude's five 25 s, one after the other on an idle machine of 4 CPUs** (section 5). The skill's 100 to 110 s for the five was not seen here.
186	
187	## Commands
188	
189	- The second set first on the class path, for a compile or a run: `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/default_repository/caches-one bin/fortress compile P.fss`, and the same two settings with `JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-BytecodeVerificationRemote"` for `bin/fortress run P` and for `bin/fortress junit <files>`.
190	- The base build's code over another tree's sources, without touching the base build: `java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.autohome=<tree> -Dfortress.caches=<empty folder> -cp "$(FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile <component>.fss`, from `<tree>/ProjectFortress`.
191	- Two caches' jars compared class by class with one tree's path rewritten to the other's: a 35-line Python reader of the class file's constant pool over `zipfile`, not kept.
192	- The classes of a build that name a prelude class: `grep -rl 'fortress/Compiler' ProjectFortress/build --include=*.class`, then `javap -v -p` on each to tell a class reference from a string.
193	
194	## Questions for the curator
195	
196	- **Which order of the remaining work: the review's A1 or A2.** This probe removes the doubt that A2 exists. What A2 costs beyond A1, by this probe: two rungs, perhaps three, about 200 s and a small test track in every gate, a prelude that lives to the end, and four small mechanisms (selector, caches, stamp, names table) that the prelude's deletion removes again. What it buys is the review's: the walls that only the switch shows are met one at a time on `main`. Not decided here.

1	<!-- A design review for the curator's decision, before the switch-over's work is planned, on which run-time class carries each built-in type of the interpreter's library on the compiled path (the rehearsal's walls W2, W12, W13 and W14), written 2026-11-13 by a Fable worker, reading only, with one compiled probe: nine ways from the language, the two libraries, the code generator and the run time, each shown on `ZZ32`, `Boolean`, `String` and `Float`, with what it changes, what it does for unboxed numbers, whether it can be undone, what the team's texts say by provenance, and what Scala, Kotlin, Swift and Julia do; the ways sorted, and a recommendation: the object's class carries the value and the trait stays an interface (walk's own way), with the merge of each number trait and its one object as a second step for the curator to rule on. -->
2	
3	# Which class carries a built-in type on the compiled path: the ways
4	
5	## The answer in short
6	
7	- A carrier is the JVM class whose instances are the values of a built-in type at run time. Today `FZZ32`, a class written by hand in Java, carries the prelude's `ZZ32`.
8	- The two libraries declare a built-in type in two shapes. The prelude says `trait ZZ32`, and `FZZ32` is the trait's class. The interpreter's library says `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `value object Boolean` with no trait at all.
9	- I found nine ways. Four give the type its class (A to D). Three are ruled out (E, F, G). Two are later layers for speed, not carriers (H, I).
10	- The four that count:
11	  - **A.** The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library. This is the prelude's way, whole.
12	  - **B.** The trait's class is written by hand, and an empty object stands below each trait. This is the rehearsal's hack.
13	  - **C.** The object's class carries the value. The trait stays a plain interface. The library's text does not change. This is walk's own way, brought to the compiled path.
14	  - **D.** One object per type: each number trait is merged with its one object, as `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` already are. Then C's machinery, with one name per type.
15	- The team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and the peers do not point to one way. The library as written points to C. The peers point to D. The team's later code is A's shape, but its author called it a special case "for the time being", and its own plan for unboxing is written over objects and `comprises` clauses, which is C's and D's shape.
16	- I recommend C now, and D as a second step that the curator rules on apart. C changes no line of the library, keeps walk as it is, removes W13 and W14 by construction, and closes the hole of ledger row 866. It gives up the prelude's trick of one hand-written class per type with no change in the code generator: the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload.
17	
18	## The words
19	
20	- **Built-in type.** A type whose values the language's implementation makes, not a constructor call: the numbers, `Boolean`, `Char`, the flat string, and a few Java-backed values (a reader, a writer, an array's store).
21	- **Carrier.** The JVM class of a built-in type's values on the compiled path.
22	- **Payload.** The Java value inside a carrier: an `int` in `FZZ32`, a `double` in `FRR64`, a `java.lang.String` in `FJavaString`.
23	- **Box.** A carrier object on the heap. A number is unboxed where the compiled code holds the payload itself: a JVM `double` in a local, a field or an array.
24	- **Springboard.** The class `T$DefaultTraitMethods` that the code generator writes for a trait `T`. It holds the trait's method bodies. An object's class extends the springboard of the first trait that the object extends (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:888-909`).
25	- **Stub.** A Java source file that declares, empty, the classes that the code generator will write, so that hand-written Java can extend them before any Fortress is compiled: `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`.
26	- **Closed type.** A type that no program can extend: an object, or a trait whose `comprises` clause lists its only subtypes. An open type is a trait without such a clause.
27	- **Native component.** A component declared `native component`. The specification says that inside one "the syntax and semantics are implementation dependent" (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:513-518`). The library's four are `FortressBuiltin`, `FlatString`, `Reflect` and `AnyType`.
28	
29	## What stands today
30	
31	### The prelude: a trait, and a class written by hand
32	
33	    trait ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ32\], StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\] }
34	            excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }
35	        opr +(self, other:ZZ32): ZZ32 = jIntOverflowingAdd(self,other)
36	        ...
37	    end
38	
39	(`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:662`.) Beside it, in Java:
40	
41	    public final class FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods
42	            implements fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32 {
43	        final int val;
44	        public int getValue() {return val;}
45	        public static FZZ32 make(int x) { return new FZZ32(x); }
46	        public RTTI getRTTI() { return RTTIc.ONLY; }
47	    }
48	
49	(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:14-43`.)
50	
51	- The code generator writes the interface `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` and its springboard from the trait.
52	- `FZZ32` extends that springboard. So the Java build needs the stub file.
53	- A table says that the type `ZZ32` is written `FZZ32` in every descriptor: `compiler/NamingCzar.java:587-601`, and a copy for the run in `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:294-306`.
54	- The class of `Box[\ZZ32\]` is named with the carrier: `Box⟦com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32⟧` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:56`).
55	- Fifteen names are carried so: `Boolean`, `Character`, `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32`, `RR64`, `JavaString`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`, `ZZ32Vector`, `StringVector` and `()`.

57	The prelude's trait is open. A program may write `object MyNum extends ZZ32`. The checker takes it, the compile exits 0, and the run dies: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: class OpenZ$MyInt can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface'. Ledger row 866 holds this. I ran it again today (section "The probe").

59	### The interpreter's library: five shapes
60	
61	1. **A trait with one native object below it.** Five types.

64	               excludes { ZZ64, ZZ, NN64, NN32 }

The revival made these (P-164, P-169, F-330, F-333).

84	Under walk, a native object's values come from a Java class of the object's own name. `BuildNativeEnvironment.nativeConstructor` builds the class name from the component's line `private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"` and the object's name (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-57`; `FortressBuiltin.fss:15-16`). So walk's rule is: **in a native component, a class written by hand is the object's class.** `glue/prim/Int.java` is `Int`'s, and its values are `FInt` objects.

86	Walk already treats `Int` and `ZZ32` as one type where it matters. It reads a value of `Int` at `ZZ32` where it infers a static argument, so `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, and it prints `ZZ32` (F-344, F-328).

88	## What the rehearsal met
89	
90	The rehearsal of 2026-11-10 switched a scratch tree's compiled path onto the interpreter's library (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`). Four of its walls are this design.
91	
92	- **W2.** The wrappers of the helper classes cannot name a class for `FortressLibrary$String` or `FortressLibrary$ZZ32`. Behind that: thirteen hand-written classes extend the prelude's springboards by name; five carried types are objects, and a hand-written class cannot extend an object; the stores have no Fortress value; `FlatString`'s classes cannot be stubbed in Java.
93	- **W12.** A carried type has two names at run time. The trait's `RTTIc` holds the trait's interface. The descriptors hold the carrier. A static argument read from a value named the first; the classes were made under the second.
94	- **W13.** `asFloat` has no body on a compiled `ZZ32`: the trait declares it, the object `Int` defines it, and the carrier was the trait's class.
95	- **W14.** `Float extends RR64` became an interface that extends the class `FRR64`: the code generator names a carried type by its carrier in an `extends` clause too.
96	
97	The rehearsal's hack for W2 turned the five objects into traits with `comprises { XCarrier }` and an empty object. That broke walk in the scratch tree. Its hack for W13 copied `asFloat` into `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and made `Float` a trait.
98	
99	All four walls come from one mismatch: the prelude's way puts the class on the trait, and the interpreter's library puts the values on the object.

105	### Way A. The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library
106	
107	This is the prelude's way, carried over whole.
108	
109	**On `ZZ32`.** The library's text changes:

112	            excludes { ZZ64, ZZ, NN64, NN32, ... }
113	        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
114	        getter asString(): String = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToString")

121	            implements fortress.FortressLibrary.ZZ32 { final int val; ... }

125	**On `String`.** `String` stays a trait with its three plain objects. `FlatString` becomes a trait that `FJavaString` carries. This is the prelude's `trait JavaString extends String`.

127	**On `Float`.** `Float`'s 146 lines move into `trait RR64`, over the bodies that `RR64` has today. `FRR64` carries `RR64`.

129	**The rule that blocks it.** A trait is open. An object excludes every type that it does not extend; a trait excludes only what its `excludes` clause lists. When the rehearsal made the five objects traits, the apis failed the overloading check with 15 errors, such as 'Invalid overloading of || in trait FlatString: (FlatString, Char)->String and (String, Number)->String' (its W2). The prelude gets around this by writing an `excludes` list on every built-in trait by hand: `trait NN64 ... excludes { ZZ32, ZZ64, RR32, RR64, NN32, ZZ }` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:818`). Steele called this "quadratic blow-up" in 2016 (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:356-365`). And the lists do not close the type: row 866.

131	**What it changes.**
132	
133	- The library's text: five objects deleted, five objects made traits, about 180 lines moved, an `excludes` list on each of ten traits. The `comprises` clauses of the five number traits go.

135	- The code generator: nothing new for the carriers. The tables are renamed.
136	- The run-time classes: thirteen classes re-parented, three stub files, as the rehearsal did.
137	- The loader: no change.
138	- The tests: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk` and each test that names `Int`, `Float` or the others as a type. The checker's count and the distance must reach 0 again after the `excludes` lists.

140	**Speed later.** It hinders. An unboxed `RR64` needs the compiler to know that a value of static type `RR64` is exactly one class. An open trait does not say so, so the code generator would have to treat the fifteen names as special for ever, against the checker's own view. Dispatch on a built-in type tests one final class, as today.
141	
142	**Undo.** Costly. The library's and walk's text are rewritten. Going back means writing the objects again.
143	
144	**The team's texts.** For: the prelude's source and the run time are this way, built alike for all its types from 2009 to 2012. Against: its author called it a special case for the time being; the reasons that made the prelude's types traits are gone; the specification calls a primitive a value object. The section "What the team's texts say" gives each with its date.

176	### Way C. The object's class carries the value, and the trait stays an interface
177	
178	This is walk's way, brought to the compiled path. The library's text does not change.
179	
180	**On `ZZ32`.** The declarations stay as they are today. The code generator compiles them as it compiles any trait and object, with one addition for a native object:
181	
182	    interface fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32                      (from trait ZZ32)
183	    final class fortress/FortressBuiltin$Int implements ...$ZZ32 (from value object Int)
184	        final int val;
185	        static Int make(int)        int getValue()

187	- The carrier is `Int`'s class. It has `asFloat`'s body, because `Int` declares it. So W13 does not arise.
188	- `Int extends ZZ32` names the interface, as every `extends` clause does. Nothing extends a carrier, because nothing extends an object. So W14 does not arise.
189	- A table gives each native object its payload: `Int` an `int`, `Float` a `double`, `FlatString` a `java.lang.String`, `BigNum` a `BigInteger`. This is the table of `NamingCzar` today, keyed by the object.
190	- One rule answers W12: a value of a native object is read at its trait where a static argument is formed, and the stamped class is named by the carrier. Walk has this rule (F-344). The checker already lets a value of `trait T comprises { O }` stand where `O` is expected (the rehearsal's W7).
191	- A value of static type `ZZ32` is exactly an `Int`, because the trait says `comprises { Int }`. So a descriptor for `ZZ32` may name `Int`'s class, as a descriptor names `FZZ32` today. The cast that row 307 asks for is the same knowledge.
192	
193	**On `Boolean`.** `value object Boolean` compiles to its own class, with a `boolean` payload. Its methods written in Fortress (`cond`, `generate`, `=`) are the object's methods. No trait, no second name.
194	
195	**On `String`.** `String` is an interface. `FlatString`'s class holds a `java.lang.String`. `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` are plain classes. A helper's Java `String` result becomes a `FlatString` value. The wrapper generator reads a helper's Java `String` parameter as the trait `String` (`NamingCzar.java:484`), so the wrapper casts it to `FlatString`'s class: the rehearsal's new converter. The cast is safe because the library's bindings pass a `FlatString` there: walk refuses a helper parameter declared `String` other than `self` (the skill's `references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The table could read such a parameter as `FlatString` instead. This is the same in every way.
196	
197	**On `Float`.** `Float`'s class holds a `double` and has its 146 lines as its own methods. `RR64` is an interface. A call `x + y` on two `RR64` values dispatches to `Float`'s `+`, as under walk.
198	
199	**Where the class comes from: three forms.** This choice is inside way C.
200	
201	1. Written by hand, extending the object's generated springboard, as `FZZ32` extends the trait's today. It needs the stub files, and `FlatString` cannot be stubbed in Java (the rehearsal's W2: Java allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`).
202	2. Written by the code generator, over a small payload class written by hand: `abstract class FZZ32 extends FValue { final int val; getValue() }`, and the generated `Int extends FZZ32`. No stub is needed, because the hand-written class extends nothing generated. The run time's Java keeps a name to test, as `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:38` tests `instanceof FZZ32`. The object then takes its traits' default methods by forwarding methods, which the code generator already writes for every trait after the first (`CodeGen.java:888-909`).
203	3. Written whole by the code generator, with the payload as a hidden field. The run time's Java then reaches the payload through a small interface.
204	
205	Form 2 looks best to me: no stubs, and the box's chain of constructors is three classes, `Int`, `FZZ32`, `FValue`. Today's chain through the one library's springboards is six, which leaves a margin of two frames before HotSpot stops removing temporary boxes (F-302). Not measured.
206	
207	**What blocks it.** The code generator compiles an object without value parameters as a singleton, one instance. A native object has many values. The specification leaves a native component's meaning to the implementation, and walk uses that freedom in the same place. So the block is in the code generator only, and it gets around it as walk does: by the component's `native` mark and a table.

212	- Walk: nothing.

291	`ZZ32` is `java.lang.Integer`, `String` is `java.lang.String`, as Kotlin does for a boxed `Int`.

348	- They became traits on 2009-03-30, by Maessen (`76c267f987`), to nest them and to put the literals below: `trait ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, `object IntLiteral extends ZZ32`. The commit's message is about error messages; the reason is in the diff.
349	- Chase flattened them on 2009-08-31 (`6896886fbc`): `trait ZZ32 extends Number`. The traits stayed traits.
350	- The later types followed the pattern: `Char` (Naden, 2011-06-16, `7bc4e5e597`; renamed `Character` by Steele, `c2c769094c`), `JavaBufferedReader` and `JavaBufferedWriter` (Steele, 2011-07-12, `1238ab95e6`: "new primitive types"), `trait JavaString extends String` (Steele, 2011-11-17, `2eb54ef20a`; until then the prelude had one carried `trait String`, as `796b6d3da5` of 2011-11-14 still shows, so Steele split it into the interpreter's shape, a `String` above a flat leaf), `NN32` (Tristan, 2011-11-23, `25f7cf9132`), `ZZ` and `NN64` (Tristan, 2012-01-03, `b22c4ac561`).
351	- Chase's paper on the mapping, in the tree from 2012-05-21 (`4a839480fc`): "For the time being, some primitive types are treated as special cases" (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:91-92`), above the table of `FZZ32` and the others. The same paper gives the rule for every other type: a trait is an interface, an object is a final class (`:78-83`).
352	- The comment on the table's test: 'arguably that is a bug in how these are defined' (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:605-610`).
353	- Steele's talk of 2016 shows the built-in types as traits and names the `excludes` lists as the problem of that shape (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:345-372`).
354	
355	### Is the prelude's carrier the team's later decision, type by type (P-37)
356	
357	P-37 says that the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision. P-26 says what counts: code "where the team built it alike for all its types" counts, and code "that its author called a stub", or that works around a limit, does not.
358	
359	The prelude's carrier has two parts, and they answer differently.
360	
361	- **The class: a final class that holds one JVM primitive, with `make` and `getValue`.** Later, built alike for all the types, and kept by every way here. Yes, it is the team's later decision, and ways A to D all take it.
362	- **The class put on a trait, with no object.** Later in date for every type. But I read it as not a decision of the language, for four reasons: its author called it a special case "for the time being" (2012); the number traits became traits to nest and to hold the literals, and both reasons are gone from both libraries; the open trait lets a program break the run (row 866); and the team's own unboxing plan has no case for it. P-26 has a clause on each side here, so the reading is the curator's to rule.
363	
364	By type:
365	
366	- `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32`, `RR64`: an object first (`b2880c05c2`, 2009-03-03), a trait from `76c267f987` (2009-03-30), flat from `6896886fbc` (2009-08-31). The interpreter's `Int`, `Long`, `Float` and `RR32` are of 2008. Later in date; the trait form came from nesting and literals. Not a later decision, in my reading.
367	- `Boolean`: a trait in the prelude from 2009-04-15 at the latest (`bfa396091b`, Flood). The interpreter's object is of 2007. The same reading.
368	- `Character`: a trait from `7bc4e5e597` (2011-06-16). The interpreter's `Char` is of 2007. The carrier: the same reading. The name `Character` is Steele's later word, 'as in Fortress spec 1.0 beta' (`c2c769094c`); it is outside this review.
369	- `String` and `JavaString`: the two libraries agree. `String` is a trait, and a flat leaf holds a Java string: the prelude's `JavaString`, the library's `FlatString`, which Maessen renamed from `JavaString` on 2009-01-05 (`5335ab745d`). The prelude came to this shape late, on 2011-11-17 (`2eb54ef20a`), so here the prelude's later decision is the interpreter's own shape. Nothing to take but the trait form of the leaf: the same reading.
370	- `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`: traits by Tristan, 2011-11-23 and 2012-01-03, on the pattern. The interpreter's objects are of July 2008. The same reading.
371	- `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`: Steele, 2011-07-12. Already taken: P-164 gave the one library the prelude's two traits by name and method. Under way C their carrier is the private object's class, not the trait's.
372	- `ZZ32Vector`, `StringVector`: Flood, 2011-09-07 (`24717d4adf`). The one library has arrays in their place (P-84, P-85). Nothing to take.
373	- `()`: `FVoid` on both sides. No question.
374	
375	## The peers
376	
377	Context only.
378	
379	- **Scala.** `Int` is declared `final abstract class Int extends AnyVal`: one final type, no interface above it. The compiler maps it to a JVM `int` and boxes it to `java.lang.Integer` where it meets `Any` or a type parameter. A value class (`class Meter(val v: Double) extends AnyVal`) is a one-field wrapper that the compiler erases to its field.
380	- **Kotlin.** `Int` is a final class of the standard library with intrinsic members. It is a JVM `int` where it is not nullable and not a type argument, and a `java.lang.Integer` elsewhere. `@JvmInline value class` is the one-field wrapper.
381	- **Swift.** `struct Int { var _value: Builtin.Int64 }` in the standard library: a struct over a compiler's builtin type, with its operators written in the library over builtin operations, and protocols joined by extension. This is way E with a real bottom type, which Fortress lacks.
382	- **Julia.** `primitive type Int64 <: Signed 64 end`: a concrete, final leaf below abstract types (`Signed`, `Integer`, `Real`, `Number`). Only an abstract type can have subtypes. Arrays of such leaves are stored inline, and code is specialised for each concrete type.
383	
384	All four make the built-in type itself one final, concrete type: way D's shape. Julia's abstract types above a final leaf are way C's and D's shape for `Number` and `AnyIntegral`. None has a second name for the same values. Scala and Kotlin show way H over it.
385	
386	## The ways sorted
387	
388	**Ruled out.**
389	
390	- E, for the numbers: it does not end, since the payload's type needs a carrier too. It stays the library's way for `Ratio`, the I/O objects and the arrays.
391	- F: every value must implement `Any` and answer its RTTI, and a JDK class cannot.
392	- G: P-37 deletes the prelude, and row 18.
393	- B: it breaks walk or makes the two paths read two texts (P-37), and no text of the team shows it.
394	
395	**Not carriers.** H and I are the layers of phase 6. They need a closed type and one canonical name. They are reasons among A to D, not alternatives to them.
396	
397	**Standing: A, C, D.** Where the three grounds point:
398	
399	- The team's later word. The prelude's code is A's shape. Its author's paper calls that shape a special case for the time being, and gives "an object is a final class" as the rule. The team's unboxing plan is C's and D's shape. So the later word splits: the later code says A, the later texts say C or D.
400	- The library as the team wrote it. C: it is the only way that changes none of its lines. Inside the library, `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` are D's shape, and the five split traits are C's.
401	- The peers. D.
402	
403	They do not agree on one way. They agree on this much: the value's class belongs to a closed, final type. A is the only standing way that does not give that.
404	
405	## Against the rehearsal's question and the plan review's section 7
406	
407	I read the rehearsal's last section and section 7 of `explorations/reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md` only after the list above was written. Where the lists differ:
408	
409	- **The rehearsal lists three ways.** Its (i) is my A, its (ii) my B, its (iii) my C in form 1, "the code generator lets a hand-written class be an object's class". It has no D, and none of E to I.
410	- **It calls (iii) new work without a precedent.** Walk has done it since 2007, and the specification's native components allow it. That changes its weight: C is the library's and walk's own design, not a third invention.
411	- **It gives the prelude's design as "one of the late positions on the compiled number tower".** The late position that the skill lists is the tower's flat shape (2009 and 2010), which P-43 took. The carrier's form is another matter, with its own history: an object first, a trait to nest, and a special case "for the time being" in 2012. So the rehearsal's sentence gives way A more weight than the sources do.
412	- **It does not ask whether the split of the five number traits still serves anything.** That is my way D and my third question.
413	- **It does not name the three forms of the class under C.** They matter for the plan review's section 7.
414	- **The plan review, 7.1: "One build serves one library", because the thirteen value classes extend the prelude's generated classes by name.** That holds for hand-written carriers that extend generated classes: ways A and B, and C in form 1. Under C in form 2 or 3, the hand-written part is a payload class that names no library, and the code generator writes the carrier. Then the one library's carriers can stand on `main` beside the prelude's thirteen, with no second set of re-parented classes and no stub files; the tables still follow the world. So the review's option A2 may cost less than its "2 or 3 rungs more for the second set", and its probe Y has a cheaper form to try first: one native object, `Int`, compiled over a payload class in a scratch tree. By reading; not built.
415	- **The plan review sizes the carriers as "a design first and then about three rungs".** I kept that figure for way C. For ways A and B it leaves out the library's and walk's rewriting.
416	- **Both hold that none keeps today's behaviour.** I agree for the compiled path, and add that C keeps walk's.
417	
418	## Recommendation
419	
420	Take way C now, in its form 2, and put way D to the curator as a second decision, after a probe. Way C compiles the library that the team wrote without changing a line of it, leaves walk alone, removes W13 and W14 by construction, answers W12 with the rule that walk already has (F-344), and closes row 866, because the checker reads the library's `comprises { Int }`. It gives the last phase what it needs for an unboxed `RR64` in a field, in an array and across a call: a type that the language itself closes. It can be undone at the cost of the code generator's table. What it gives up: the prelude's economy, where a hand-written class extends a trait's springboard and the code generator knows nothing; under C the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload and many values, about three rungs by reading, and the thirteen run-time classes change in any case. It also keeps two names for five number types, `ZZ32` and `Int`, with one rule on each path to hold them together. Way D removes that rule and about 50 dead bodies, and matches every peer, but it rewrites text of the team's whose reasons are gone and not whose authorship is; it should wait for one probe, the checker's count and walk's suites on a library with `ZZ32` and `RR64` merged, and for the curator's reading of P-26 on the split.
421	
422	## The probe
423	
424	One compiled program, under the prelude, on `/home/user/fortress` at `6468aa6ec7`, with a private copy of the caches. Machine: nproc 4, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, load 0.2.
425	
426	    object MyInt extends ZZ32
427	      getter asString(): String = "MyInt"
428	    end
429	    f(x: ZZ32): String = x.asString
430	    run(): () = do
431	      println(f(3))
432	      z: ZZ32 = MyInt
433	      println(f(z))
434	    end
435	
436	    $ ../../bin/fortress compile OpenZ.fss      (exit 0, no message)
437	    $ ../../bin/fortress run OpenZ
438	    Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class OpenZ$MyInt can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface
439	
440	This is row 866, reproduced. It is W14's cause, reached by a program under the prelude.
441	
442	## Report items
443	
444	### Defects
445	
446	None new. Row 866 reproduced (above). The rehearsal's W4, W12, W13 and W14 are its own findings; this review adds no row.
447	
448	### Sentences of the specification made false
449	
450	None. This review changes no text.
451	
452	### Decisions
453	
454	- I listed ways H and I as layers, not as carriers. The alternative was to rank them beside A to D. The evidence: a box class is needed wherever a value meets `Any` or a type parameter, in Scala and Kotlin too, and PLAN puts unboxed arithmetic in phase 6 (decision B).
455	- I ran the probe with a private copy of the caches (`-Dfortress.caches`), so that the shared caches stayed as they were while another probe ran. No decision of the curator covers it.
456	- I did not probe way D's merge. It needs a build of walk's Java, which this task may not make.
457	
458	### Points to report: where the record or the rehearsal turned out wrong
459	
460	1. **The rehearsal, W14, "no row".** Row 866 holds the same cause, a carried type's class named as a superinterface, for a program's object under the prelude. The rehearsal's sentence "In the prelude nothing extends a carried trait in Fortress source" is true of the prelude's own source and misses that a program can.
461	2. **The rehearsal, W2.** It presents the five objects as the one library's departure from the prelude's traits. The history runs the other way: the prelude's number types were objects first (`b2880c05c2`, 2009-03-03) and became traits to nest and to hold literals (`76c267f987`). And its question "whether the five objects stay objects, with the code generator taught to let a hand-written class be an object's class" names as new what walk has done since 2007 (`BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-57`).
462	3. **The rehearsal, W12.** It says the prelude "never infers a static argument from a carried type's RTTI". The team met the same two names under walk in 2008 (`fca589bbb0`), and the revival's walk holds the rule that answers it (F-344). The rehearsal cites neither.
463	4. **F-18.** It says that the team's direction for unboxing "builds on this class per instantiation (the plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` ...)". `Unbox.java` says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. It plans the bits of a primitive, a singleton, a struct and a `comprises` clause. The loader's stub is a separate trace.
464	5. **The rehearsal's question** calls the prelude's carrier design "one of the late positions on the compiled number tower". The late position is the flat shape (the skill's `references/exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources"; P-43), not the carrier's form.
465	6. **The plan review, 7.1**, "One build serves one library": true of hand-written carriers that extend generated classes, not of carriers that the code generator writes over a payload class (way C, forms 2 and 3). By reading.
466	7. **PLAN's N5** holds the carriers as one rung of tables. The rehearsal already said that this is too small. This review adds that the size depends on the way: way C needs no library rung and no walk rung; ways A and B need both.
467	
468	### For FACTS
469	
470	1. The prelude's built-in number types were objects when first written (`b2880c05c2`, 2009-03-03, Flood), became traits on 2009-03-30 to nest and to hold the literal objects (`76c267f987`, Maessen), and stayed traits when the prelude was flattened (`6896886fbc`, 2009-08-31, Chase); the team's paper on the mapping calls their hand-written carriers special cases "for the time being" (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:91-92`). It means that the trait form of the prelude's carriers has no reason left in either library. Shown by `git log --full-history --reverse -S'object ZZ32' a874948ac -- ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`. Detail: this report, "What the team's texts say, by provenance".
471	2. In the interpreter's library each of the five split number traits has exactly one object since the tower is flat and the numerals have their own types; the split was made for `IntLiteral` (`fca589bbb0`) and for nesting. About 50 bodies of `trait RR64` that go through `asFloat(self)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:408-504`) can never run, since `Float`'s own are more specific for every value. It means that a merge (way D) deletes dead text, and that the compiled dispatch of an `RR64` operator has an arm that is never taken. Shown by reading; no test. Detail: this report, "Way D".
472	3. Under walk, a native component's object takes its values from a Java class of the object's name in the component's `package` (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-57`). It means that "a hand-written class is the object's class" is walk's rule, not a new one. Detail: this report, "The interpreter's library: five shapes".
473	
474	### Commands
475	
476	- The first commit that holds a text, across the cut history: `git log --full-history --reverse --format='%h %ad %an %s' --date=short -S'TEXT' a874948ac -- PATH | head -1`. Without `head`, the conversion's snapshot roots print hundreds of unrelated commits.
477	- A compiled run that leaves the shared caches alone: `cp -a default_repository/caches tmp/X/caches`, then `export FORTRESS_CACHES=$PWD/tmp/X/caches JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$PWD/tmp/X/caches"` before `bin/fortress compile` and `bin/fortress run`.
478	
479	### Questions for the curator
480	
481	**1. Which run-time class carries each built-in type of the one library on the compiled path?** A decision not taken.
482	
483	- The sources and their dates: the interpreter's library (2007 to 2008, Maessen, Ryu, Steele, Flood); the specification's value objects, api style and native components (the Working Draft of February 2011); Chase's unboxing plan (2009-03-11); the prelude and its run-time classes (2009 to 2012, Flood, Maessen, Chase, Steele, Naden, Tristan), which is the team's later code; Chase's paper on the mapping (2012), which calls those classes special cases for the time being. None is one of the type group's late positions that the skill lists: the late position on the compiled number tower is its flat shape, which P-43 took, not the form of its carriers. The later works checked: the POPL 2019 paper's extract and Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016 say nothing on carriers; the 2016 talk shows the built-in types as traits and names the cost of their `excludes` lists.
484	- The solutions: way A (the prelude's, whole: library and walk rewritten), way C (the object's class carries; the library and walk unchanged; the code generator learns the payload), way D (C, with each number trait merged into its one object).
485	- Which keeps the current behaviour: under walk, C. On the compiled path nothing does, since the prelude is deleted; A is nearest to the prelude's run time.
486	
487	**2. Under P-26, is the prelude's trait form of a carried type a later decision of the team's, or code that serves only the implementation?** A decision not taken; it decides between A and the others. The evidence for each side is in "Is the prelude's carrier the team's later decision".
488	
489	**3. If C: are the five number traits merged with their objects (way D)?** A decision not taken. It changes text that the team wrote, for reasons that are gone. The probe that it needs first: the checker's count, the distance and walk's suites on a library with the merge.

1	<!-- A design review for the curator's decision on how a number compared by `=` with a numeral of the same value comes to answer `true` on both paths under the static numerals (ledger rows 973 and 966, F-346, F-341, review-queue item 487), written 2026-11-10 by a Fable review worker on the code of `9a0f69e01a` (base build `/home/user/fortress-base31`, a worktree seeded from it): a primer, where each path stands with runs, one measurement of the compiled checker against the one library, how the library avoids the question for `+` and `<`, why it declares `=` over `Any`, the team's sources, the peers, six ways with what each changes, sees, keeps, bends and costs, how they weigh, and the recommendation. Nothing in the original tree and no entry of the record was edited; every run used a worktree of its own. -->
2	
3	# A number `=` a numeral: the ways to `true`, for your decision
4	
5	This review is for you, the curator. The result is not in question: your design gives `u = 0` the answer `true` for a zero `u: NN32` (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`, section 11). The question is by which rule or which library text both paths get there.
6	
7	- **Tree.** The code of `9a0f69e01a`. `main` moved while I worked, but `git diff --stat 9a0f69e01a HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library` is empty at `0a6abca6f0`.
8	- **What it builds on.** Rows 973 and 966, F-346, F-341, the static numerals probe's question 1 (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-30/probes/draft-numerals.md`, section 13), climb batch 29b's point for you (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29b.md`, "The point for him in the morning") and its review (`explorations/reviews/batch-29b-review.md`, section 2).
9	- **What is new here.** One measurement that the record held only by reading: what the compiled checker does with `u = 0` against the one library (section 2.3). Three kin cases run on both paths: a program's own number type, a value typed `Any` or `Number`, a `case` clause. Two probes of ways: the library without its `=` over `Any` (way A), and a generic fallback (way E).
10	
11	**Words used in this review**
12	
13	- **Walk**: the interpreter, `bin/fortress P.fss`. **The compiled path**: `bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`.
14	- **The one library**: the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`). **The prelude**: the compiled path's own library today (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`). **The switch-over**: the step at which the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted (P-37).
15	- **The checker**: the compiled path's static type checker. Walk does not run it until after the switch-over (P-12).
16	- **A numeral**: a number written in digits, as `0` or `0.5`. **Its default**: the type it takes where nothing fixes one: `ZZ32` (or `ZZ64`, `ZZ` by its value), and `RR64` with a radix point (P-173).
17	- **The fallback `=`**: the one library's top-level `opr =(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = a SEQV b` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:96`). **`SEQV`**: strict equivalence, which is `false` for two values of different types (P-168).
18	- **A type's own `=`**: the `=` that a type declares on itself, as `NN32`'s `opr =(self, b:NN32)` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:449`).
19	- **A pair**: an `=` between two different number types, as `ZZ64`'s `opr =(self, b:ZZ32)` (F-324).
20	- **Promotion**: a generic call `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` runs at the narrowest type into which both arguments convert (P-74, P-46).
21	- **A rung**: one task of a climb batch. **P-N**, **F-N**, **row N**: an entry of POSITIONS, of FACTS, a row of the gap ledger.

23	## 1. The question, and a primer
24	
25	**The question.** Under the static numerals, by which rule of the language or which text of the library does `u = 0` answer `true`, and `u =/= 0` answer `false`, for a number `u` equal to the numeral, on both paths, before and after the switch-over?
26	
27	### 1.1 Why the question exists at all
28	
29	A numeral has no value of its own when a program runs (P-174). Before the program runs, it becomes a value of some number type. Which type depends on where it stands (P-173):
30	
31	    u: NN32 = 0      (* the place fixes NN32: the numeral becomes the NN32 zero *)
32	    x = 0            (* nothing fixes a type: the numeral takes its default, the ZZ32 zero *)
33	    a: Any = 0       (* Any fixes no type either: the ZZ32 zero *)
34	
35	The number types are siblings. An `NN32` zero and a `ZZ32` zero are two different values, and `SEQV` says so: `false`.
36	
37	In `u = 0`, the numeral stands as an argument of the operator `=`. The one library declares many `=`. Two of them matter here:
38	
39	    opr =(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = a SEQV b       (* the fallback, FortressLibrary.fss:96 *)
40	    opr =(self, b: NN32): Boolean = ...             (* NN32's own, FortressBuiltin.fss:449 *)
41	
42	- For the fallback, the second parameter is `Any`. `Any` fixes no type, so the numeral takes its default and arrives as a `ZZ32`. The fallback then compares an `NN32` with a `ZZ32`: `false`.
43	- For `NN32`'s own `=`, the second parameter is `NN32`. That fixes a type, so the numeral arrives as the `NN32` zero: `true`.
44	
45	Both declarations can take the call. The tree's rule picks the fallback, because the numeral reaches it without a coercion, and "a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits" (P-46; P-49 for the checker's order). So the tree answers `false`, and your design answers `true`.
46	
47	### 1.2 What does not have the problem
48	
49	    u + 0        (* NN32's + : the numeral becomes an NN32 *)
50	    u < 0        (* NN32's < : the same *)
51	    z = 0        (* for z: ZZ32: the default is ZZ32, so ZZ32's own = fits as it is *)
52	    x = 0        (* for x: RR64: the pair =(RR64, ZZ32) fits the default as it is *)
53	
54	Only a type whose own `=` the default does not fit has the problem: `NN32`, `NN64` and `RR32` beside an integer numeral, `QQ` and `RR32` beside a numeral with a radix point, and every number type of a program's own.
55	
56	## 2. Where each path stands today
57	
58	Each line below is a run of mine unless it cites the record. The programs are small probes, kept in my transcript and not committed.
59	
60	### 2.1 Walk, on the one library
61	
62	For `u: NN32 = 0`, `h: QQ = 1/2`, `y: Byte = 7` (a program's own value object with a numeral coercion and its own `=`), `a: Any = u`, `m: Number = u`, `z: ZZ32 = 0`, `x: RR64 = 0`:
63	
64	    u = 0: false          0 = u: false         u =/= 0: true        h = 0.5: false
65	    y = 7 (Byte): false   7 = y (Byte): false

110	## 3. How the library avoids the question elsewhere, and why `=` is different
111	
112	**`u + 0`, `u < 0`.** The one library declares `+` and `<` only as methods of self-typed traits: `opr +(self, other: T): T` in `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:361`), `opr <(self, other: T)` in `StandardPartialOrder[\T\]` (`:230`), and each number type's own. No `+` or `<` takes `Any`. So no declaration fits `(NN32, numeral at its default)` as it is, the coercion attempt runs, and the numeral converts to `NN32`. Nothing special is done for numerals: the absence of a catch-all does the work.
113	
114	**`=`.** `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =(self, other:T): Boolean = self SEQV other` in the same self-typed form (`:100-102`), and `StandardPartialOrder` extends it (`:222-223`, `:232`). But beside them stands the catch-all, the fallback over `(Any, Any)` (`:96`), and `=/=` exists only as a catch-all, `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a=b)` (`:98`), except on `QQ`, `RR32` and `Float`. A numeral at its default fits a catch-all as it is. That is the whole difference.
115	
116	**Why the library declares `=` over `Any`, with its history.**
117	
118	- 2007-01-04, the first import of the interpreter's library (`72ae6881b1`, git author `jm143038`): `opr =(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = false` and `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a=b)` (`ProjectFortress/FortressLibrary.fss:64-65` there). The fallback meant: two values with no `=` of their own are unequal.
119	- 2008-03-04 (`d56a402b41`, git author `jmaessen`, "Preliminary (unsatisfactory) implementation of SEQUIV"): the body became `a SEQUIV b`. Two days later (`21946c933f`) the operator was respelled `SEQV`.
120	- The compiler's prelude, the team's later library, never had it: it declares `===` for a few types (`64e5f04dbf`, 2010-05-05, git author `dr2chase`, "Added definition of === for popular types") and `=` only on its types.
121	- The revival kept the fallback and gave it its meaning in P-168: "Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence". P-165 and F-324 lean on it: two numbers that no coercion joins compare by the fallback and answer `false` without an error.
122	
123	What the fallback is for: generic code. A `List[\E\]` compares its elements by `=` with `E` unbounded; `assert(x, y, msg)` and `=/=` compare any two values (F-280); a value object without its own `=` is still comparable. Section 6, way A, measures how much of the library stands on it.

125	## 4. The team's sources
126	
127	**The Working Draft on numerals** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-148`). A numeral has a numeral type (`:83-129`). "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because, as in common mathematical usage, we expect them to be polymorphic" (`:132-134`). "This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`:142-144`), and the libraries "define coercions from numerals to integers ... and rational numbers" (`:146-148`). The Draft says nothing of a numeral compared with a number. It has no default.
128	
129	**The Draft on which declaration a call takes** (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:450-456`, "Coercion Resolution"): "we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added". This is the rule that P-46 and P-49 keep.
130	
131	**The Draft on `=`.** It declares no `=` over `Any`. `Any` has only `===` (`basic-lib/objects.tex:22-24`). `=` is a method of a self-typed trait, `opr =(self, other: T)` in `IdentityEquality[\T\]`, with the property that it agrees with strict equivalence (`advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:134-139`), and each number type lists its own, as `opr =(self, other: ZZ)` (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:144`) and `opr =(self, other: QQ)` (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:133`). The operators chapter says only: "The expression `e =/= e'` is semantically equivalent to the expression `NOT (e = e')`" (`basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-263`), and that `<`, `<=`, `>=`, `>` "are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types" (`:271-273`), with no word on a numeral operand.
132	
133	**Put together.** In the Draft's own language, `u = 0` has no declaration that applies without coercion, because nothing takes `Any`. So the coercion is added, the numeral becomes an `NN32`, and the answer is `true`. The Draft reaches your result through the shape of its library, not through a rule about numerals. The interpreter's catch-all is what breaks it, and the catch-all is the interpreter's own, from 2007, not the Draft's.
134	
135	**The revived specification** records today's state as a departure, not as the rule: "the interpreter answers `u = 0` false ... and whether `u = 0` is true is open" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5278-5290`; `:3813-3825` for `=/=`). Its literals chapter already says that "the parameter types of the declaration that a call invokes" are places that fix a type (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:202-204`). Its coercion chapter says the opposite for the choice: "a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its conversion into any other type is a coercion" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:111-114`). The revival wrote both.

137	## 5. The peers, as context only
138	
139	- **Haskell, Rust, Swift.** A literal is polymorphic; `==` takes two operands of one type, so `u == 0` types the literal at `u`'s type. The default (`Integer`, `i32`, `Int`) applies only when nothing constrains the literal. None has an `==` over a top type. This is the Draft's shape (way A).
140	- **C#.** A constant expression converts implicitly to the other operand's type when its value fits, so `u == 0` compares two `uint`. A rule for constants at operators (way C).
141	- **Go.** An untyped constant takes the other operand's type in a binary operation, and its default type only where none is given. Go shows the `Any` case exactly: for `var a interface{} = uint32(0)`, `a == 0` is `false`, because the constant becomes an `int`. Every way below keeps that answer for `a: Any`.
142	- **Julia.** No polymorphic literals; `UInt32(0) == 0` is `true` because `==` on numbers compares values across types (way F).
143	- **Scala 2, Java.** `==` over the top type, with special cases for boxed numbers. Scala 3 added a restriction on `==` across unrelated types (`CanEqual`), a move toward way A.
